paras.en: Macron stated in a TV interview that “soldiers, radars, defence systems” would be sent.

While he did not give specifics about volumes, it was a move described by French newspaper Le Monde as marking “a geopolitical shift”, as defence cooperation between the two countries has previously been “discreet, ambiguous and marked by extreme caution when it came to defining it”, the newspaper noted.

Last week, France’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Pascal Confavreux, said again that “operational elements” to defend Saudi oil facilities had been put into action, without specifying which “military means” had been sent.

Meanwhile, on Monday, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot met with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud, to review bilateral relations and discuss regional developments. Barrot also reaffirmed France’s solidarity with Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks.
Krieg assesses that France can offer Gulf states generally something that has become “increasingly valuable”: military capabilities not entirely dependent on the US.

“France can offer defence industrial cooperation, technology transfers, joint production, training and greater operational autonomy,” he said. “For countries such as the UAE and Qatar, this means progressively reducing their dependence on American weapons systems, spare parts, intelligence and political permissions.”
However, Krieg cautioned that the “central dilemma” for France is likely to be whether increasing its involvement in the region could draw it into the ongoing conflict.

“Consider the protection of Saudi energy infrastructure against Houthi attacks,” he said. “French air defence systems intercepting missiles would directly undermine the Houthis’ military strategy. If French forces are subsequently targeted, Paris could face pressure to retaliate. What begins as a defensive deployment could gradually become an operational commitment with much wider implications.”
Krieg explained that the same is likely to apply to naval deployments around the Strait of Hormuz, adding that “escalation in one theatre can rapidly affect another”.
France’s ties with Iran have already been strained over tit-for-tat diplomatic expulsions and political rhetoric against each other.
In July and August, France strongly condemned Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

In July, two French Embassy staff members were detained in Tehran and then declared personae non gratae. Iran’s Foreign Ministry said the diplomats had “interfered in Iran’s internal affairs under the pretext of engaging with civil society”.
In August, French Foreign Minister Barrot expelled two Iranian diplomats in retaliation.

Speaking at the Global Security Forum in the Qatari capital, Doha, on Tuesday, US Envoy Tom Barrack said that Washington is moving away from its traditional security-for-oil relationship with the Middle East and no longer seeks to dominate the region.
“The US no longer wants to own,” said Barrack, who serves as US ambassador to Turkiye and special envoy for Syria. “The bargain is not to control, but to not leave. We’re not leaving.”
Barrack acknowledged that, following months of Iranian strikes on their infrastructure, regional partners are increasingly recognising the limits of US involvement.

Across the Middle East itself, defence partnerships have grown. In August, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan signed a trilateral security pact, also known as the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. The pact has been activated amid Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
But there may now be an opening for other external actors – such as France – to find more of a role.
Krieg said Gulf states do not believe France will replace the US, whose military and intelligence infrastructure remains unmatched. Rather, they want a “diversified network of security partnerships”.

“France is particularly attractive because it possesses genuine expeditionary capabilities and has demonstrated a willingness to defend Gulf partners without joining Washington’s offensive campaign against Iran,” he said. “Its military presence has consequently acquired greater political significance.”

articles.title: Former U.S. ambassador on Trump's recent moves to embrace Russia
articles.author: Steve Inskeep

paras.en: Former U.S. ambassador on Trump's recent moves to embrace Russia
NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks with former U.S. Ambassador to Russia Michael McFaul about President Trump's latest embrace of Russia and what it means for Ukraine and any hopes of peace.

Let's ask Michael McFaul about this. He was the U.S. ambassador to Russia during the Obama administration and is now a professor of political science and a Hoover senior fellow at Stanford University, where it is ridiculously early, and yet he's gotten up to talk with us. Ambassador, welcome.
INSKEEP: And thanks for the time. The president has been so favorable to Russia that I have to ask if you think that his most recent actions amount to a shift at all.

MCFAUL: Well, you're right to remind everybody that he's liked Putin for a long time. I mean, go back to the beginning of his first administration. He constantly praised Putin. He sided with him. When questioned in a very famous summit with Putin, his first one in 2018, in Helsinki, he sided with Putin and he didn't side with our own intelligence community about whether there was interference in our elections.

So that piece has been consistent. What I think has changed in a profound way in the last week - in a profound, tragic way for me - is he always had a few constraints. He always was talking to Zelenskyy. He claimed from Day 1 of this second term that he wanted to end the war in Ukraine. And I applaud him for that, by the way. Everybody should want to see the end of this barbaric war that Putin started. But this week felt different in both tone and actions.

So rhetorically, he's always sided with Putin. Now he really doubled down. As Emily just went through that list, every single one of those things are concessions to Putin. That's not a way to mediate. He's not mediating. He's just giving Putin what he wants. And then when it comes to Zelenskyy, he's blaming Zelenskyy for Putin killing his own people. And I thought that clip you just played of the Ukrainian woman, it's a former press secretary of President Zelenskyy, who's now defected, gone - you know, just doesn't support Zelenskyy anymore, I should be clear...
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: MCFAUL: I think you just see the true colors of President Trump right now.

INSKEEP: Well, Zelenskyy spoke with this bipartisan group of American lawmakers yesterday, and he posted a video online afterward of his address. He said the Pentagon is making it harder for Ukraine to get intelligence and also delaying the U.S. approval of the transfer of weapons. Let's listen to some of that.
PRESIDENT VOLODYMYR ZELENSKYY: All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us. And this is in sharp contrast to what we are achieving on the battlefield.

INSKEEP: I want to explore that a little bit, too, because he says a political decision, suggesting it's not just Trump's impulses here or there, but that there's a deliberate change in policy by the United States. It sounds like you would agree with that.

MCFAUL: I do. And I tragically agree with that because we in this fight between democratic Ukraine and autocratic Russia, in this fight between an imperial leader in Russia who's invading and trying to reconquer a former colony, we're now on the side of the autocrats. This is unprecedented in American history. I can't think of a time when in a similar kind of situation, in 100 years, where we have decided, oh, we're going to support the autocrats, the imperialists against a country fighting for its independence with a democratically elected leader.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Now, you know, there's some ambiguity as to who made the decision about turning off Starlink. And there's some ambiguity about why there's the delays in the missiles, the interceptors that President Zelenskyy is talking about. But if we were trying to help Ukraine, we would be clearing up that ambiguity. We would be saying, this is what happened, and now we're turning it on. And Trump is doing exactly the opposite.
INSKEEP: Well, let's talk about some of those people.
MCFAUL: And I just find that the moral...
INSKEEP: Let's talk about some of those people in the room with Zelenskyy...
INSKEEP: ...Some of those lawmakers from both parties, some of whom face the voters...
INSKEEP: ...In a couple of weeks. What, if anything, can they do about the president's course?

MCFAUL: Well, in the short run, not much. But in the short run, I guarantee you, most of them are not going to be lining up with the president, because the public opinion polling here in America about Putin is very clear. We don't have many polls, Steve, where 80% of Americans - 83% of Americans think that Putin's a bad guy. So when Trump is embracing him, he is out of step with American society.
INSKEEP: You said in the short term. What about the longer term? Is there something Congress can do over time?

MCFAUL: Yes. I hope when there's a new Congress - and, you know, tragically, that's a long time for Ukrainians. But introduce new legislation to prevent Americans from doing business with Russia. Introduce new legislation to provide a new military assistance package to Ukraine. We haven't had that for two years. And even if President Trump vetoes it, it'll at least show what side the U.S. Congress is on.
INSKEEP: And I guess we should mention Congress did pass a law, but it allowed the president to waive it, and that's what he's done.
INSKEEP: I suppose Congress would have to pass a law with more restrictions.
INSKEEP: Ambassador McFaul, it's always a pleasure talking with you. Thank you so much.
INSKEEP: Michael McFaul is a former U.S. ambassador to Russia.

articles.title: Trump makes Russia-friendly moves as he looks for a way to end the war with Ukraine
articles.author: Emily Feng

paras.en: Trump makes Russia-friendly moves as he looks for a way to end the war with Ukraine
President Trump's up and down relationship with Russia is back on as he presses to find an end to the war in Ukraine amid high energy costs ahead of the U.S. midterms.
Democrats and Republicans are opposed to President Trump's friendlier stance toward Russia.

Senators from both parties are criticizing Trump's decision to lift diesel sanctions. The president said that move was meant to head off high energy prices ahead of the midterm elections. He's also paused sharing military intelligence with Ukraine. In a moment, we'll discuss all this with former U.S. Ambassador to Russia Michael McFaul. We begin with the news.
MARTÍNEZ: NPR's Emily Feng is with us this morning. Emily, so first, run through what President Trump has done to roll back pressure on Russia.

EMILY FENG, BYLINE: OK. Here's just a brief list. He's had the Treasury Department lift sanctions on Russian diesel. He's effectively suspended a sanctions bill he just signed into law that was named in honor of the late Senator Lindsey Graham. He said yesterday he was willing to sit down with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin to talk about the war on Ukraine even if Ukraine's leader is not there. And then he cited a Ukrainian woman he heard speak about the loss of lives as a reason to end the war.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: She blamed Zelenskyy. She said, he's killing our men. And the fact is, she said - and it was very poignant. She said, our men are dying. Our men have no legs.

FENG: Also last week, Ukrainian officials say they lost connectivity for a few days to Starshield and Starlink. These are satellite services which Ukraine uses for battlefield communications. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says he thinks the U.S. was behind that. And he also made the extraordinary move of lobbying a bipartisan group of senators and House members about this Starlink issue this week.
MARTÍNEZ: Emily, do you have any sense why Trump, who really has faced repeated accusations of favoring Russia, is now seemingly courting Russia again?

FENG: Trump wants a deal. He wants a foreign policy win in Ukraine. And he told reporters yesterday he is negotiating with Russia on a number of issues - on energy, on American hostages in Russia. And he also wants to keep Russia from - not helping Iran. So he said he doesn't want to drive Russia away from the bargaining table.
I spoke to Bill Taylor about this. He was a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine until 2009. And Taylor notes the U.S. is no longer giving much direct financial and military assistance to Ukraine.

BILL TAYLOR: I mean, it's down 95%. The only thing we continue to provide, which is very valuable - it's come up in the last couple of days - is this military intelligence and the ability for the Europeans to buy weapons from the United States and Elon Musk to be able to provide Starlink.

FENG: But now the U.S. has shown Ukraine cannot rely on the U.S. for that intelligence either. And in that meeting I mentioned with members of Congress on Monday, Zelenskyy said that the administration, the U.S. government, is the one holding up weapons for his country.
PRESIDENT VOLODYMYR ZELENSKYY: We also know that, unfortunately, the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that our partners have already paid for.

FENG: Secretary of State Marco Rubio also spoke on this. Speaking in Mumbai, India, today, Rubio said it could be accurate that a batch of interceptors purchased for Ukraine has not been delivered. Rubio, however, told reporters that the important takeaway was, quote, "there has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine."
MARTÍNEZ: All right. So, Emily, there's been a bipartisan fallout that's followed this. Tell us about that.

FENG: Yes. Notably, both Republican and Democratic lawmakers are criticizing the U.S. for buying Russian diesel. For example, on top of the lawmakers that Zelenskyy briefed, you have Republican Representative Mike Lawler saying the diesel puts money in Russia's pocket. Notably, Darline Graham, sister of the late Senator Graham, whose namesake sanctions law was just signed into law by Trump, spoke out against the U.S. buying Russian diesel. And this fallout is illustrative of the bind that Trump has put himself in by starting a seemingly intractable conflict with Iran. He has driven up energy prices for Americans. That's put more leverage in Russia's hands to push the U.S. for a quick resolution on Ukraine.

paras.en: MARTÍNEZ: All right. That's NPR's Emily Feng. Emily, thanks.

articles.title: DOJ charges 28 with voting crimes. And, TikTok ignored staff's child safety concerns
articles.author: Brittney Melton

paras.en: DOJ charges 28 with voting crimes. And, TikTok ignored staff's child safety concerns

The Justice Department has charged 28 green card holders in California with election crimes for allegedly illegally registering to vote or voting in U.S. elections. This marks a significant escalation in the Trump administration's feud with the state over its voting system as the midterm elections approach. The DOJ also filed an emergency request to prevent California from processing ballots returned by people on the voter rolls that the federal government says are "likely noncitizens." California has sought clarification on the federal government's conclusions but has not received any. Last week, the DOJ sued California and Los Angeles County after local officials refused to investigate allegations made by the administration about noncitizen voting.

Previously unreported court records show employees' frustration with leadership's response to these issues. Staff alerted management about minors engaging with sexual content, which the company profited from. paras.en: Cold and flu season in the U.S. starts this month and lasts through May, according ot the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Cooler temperatures and drier air can increase our vulnerability to illnesses like the common cold, flu, RSV and COVID-19. Get ahead of the game now by putting together a cold-and-flu prep kit. Here's what experts say you should have in your home.

- 🤒 Over-the-counter medications are good options, but always follow the recommended dosage to avoid risks or side effects. Some good medications to have include ibuprofen or naproxen, which can relieve headaches, body aches and sore throats by reducing inflammation and Acetaminophen, which can lower body temperature.

- 🤒 Honey acts as an anti-inflammatory and soothes the throat, making it useful for young children who can't take cough medicine. But don't give it to children under 12 months due to the risk of botulism.
- 🤒 A thermometer is a must-have for checking your temperature. For children 3 and under, a rectal option is preferred.
- 🤒 A saline spray or rinse for your nose can help keep the mucous membranes moist and help relieve symptoms by loosening thick mucus during a cold.

- The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists has updated its menopause treatment guidelines for the first time since 2014. The group now recommends using hormone replacement therapy along with some other treatments to alleviate symptoms.
- A wedding day can be one of the costliest days in a couple's life. Some are opting to save money by choosing grocery-store cakes over specialty bakers' cakes.

- Vegemite is such an iconic breakfast spread in Australia that a convicted killer is suing the state of Victoria for the right to eat it in prison. The state has banned Vegemite because it could potentially be used to brew alcohol and throw off dogs.

articles.title: The most beautiful sections of China's Great Wall

paras.en: Editor’s Note: Monthly Ticket is a CNN Travel series that spotlights some of the most fascinating topics in the travel world. In September, we’re celebrating superlatives as we look at some of the world’s biggest, tallest and most expensive attractions and destinations.
Having lived in Beijing for almost 12 years, I’ve had plenty of time to travel widely in China.
I’ve visited more than 100 cities, not to mention countless towns and villages throughout the mainland’s 31 provinces.

Looking back, I’ve come to realize it was my frequent visits to different parts of the Great Wall in Beijing that were a driving force behind my desire to explore the rest of the country and, along with it, the many sections of wall that lie outside the capital’s boundaries.

Work on the Great Wall began more than 2,500 years ago, its origins dating back to China’s Spring and Autumn Period of around 770 BCE to 476 BCE. Various sections were added in subsequent eras as competing dynasties and factions sought to exert their control.
Work eventually stopped in the 17th century.
Though not a single, unbroken structure, the wall spans over 21,000 kilometers, winding through 15 provinces, 97 prefectures and 404 counties.
And while certain sections have been incredibly popular among tourists, many parts have slipped into obscurity, disrepair and sometimes oblivion.

Whether you’re planning to visit the Great Wall for the first time or the 50th, the following destinations are sure to make your trip to China even more worthwhile. (Check out the above video for dramatic aerial footage of some of these amazing sites.)
The Great Wall is not simply a brick and mortar bulwark; in certain places, towers on jagged mountain peaks, fortress towns or even wide rivers count as sections of “wall.”

The Turtle City, built in the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644) as part of the Great Wall’s “Yellow River Defense Line,” was completed in 1608 and was home to around 2,000 infantrymen and 500 cavalry units during peak use.
Today, this fortress city is located in the Sitan Township of Jingtai County in north central Gansu province.
While there aren’t many real turtles in the “Turtle City,” the garrison town got its nickname due to its unique shape.

The south gate acts as the head and the west and east gates as the flippers. The town’s oval wall is the body, while the north gate acts as its tail. As one of the most well-preserved and truly authentic walled cities left in China today, it’s definitely worth your time.
Staying in the Jingtai County center is recommended. The ancient city is only a 30-minute cab ride from your lodgings, so you can visit whenever the light is best for photos.

When in Jingtai, try local specialties such as the five Buddha tofu and the Jingtai cold mixed noodles – both are spicy vegetarian dishes. A walk through the sprawling night market in Jingtai County People’s Square, which boasts more than 50 snack stalls, is also recommended for adventurous foodies.

Getting there: Lanzhou, the capital of Gansu province, has a major international airport and high-speed train connections from many cities in China. The drive to Yongtai Turtle City from downtown Lanzhou takes about 2.5 hours (195 kilometers). From Lanzhou Zhongchuan Airport, it’s only 1.5 hours (125 kilometers).
Mutianyu and Jiankou are two parts of the same Stone Dragon – two contiguous sections of the Great Wall that together stretch for roughly 25 kilometers along Beijing’s mountaintops.

Historical records show that millions of men spent centuries constructing the Great Wall. Stand atop the wall at either Mutianyu or Jiankou, and you’ll begin to comprehend the gravity of this statement.
These two sections are arguably the two most classic examples of Ming Dynasty Great Wall surviving today, and climbing either is guaranteed to be a life-changing experience.
Mutianyu is the best portion of the “tourist wall.” Restored in the 1980s, it’s very commercial but also superbly beautiful. Visitors not up for the hike can take a cable car to the top.

To the west of Mutianyu, Jiankou is colloquially known as the “wild wall” – no ticket needed and not commercialized. That being said, as of 2020, hiking at Jiankou has become somewhat frowned upon by the local government because of safety concerns.
Mutianyu and Jiankou are less than a 90-minute drive (without traffic) from downtown Beijing, yet it’s highly recommended to enjoy a night in the countryside if time allows.

Jiankou can be accessed via Xizhazi village; if dates align, you might even be able to spend a few days with William Lindesay, world-renowned Great Wall historian, and his wonderful family at The Barracks, their wall-side courtyard home.
For lodgings around Mutianyu, The Brickyard is a superbly comfortable choice.
In fall and spring, shades of the wall’s gray brick contrast with nature’s vibrant colors. Peak autumn foliage and spring cherry blossoms provide stunning backdrops for photos.
For winter sports enthusiasts, there’s skiing and skating next to the Wall at locations not far from Mutianyu.

Getting to Mutianyu: Restrictions on applying for temporary driving licenses in China were relaxed in September 2019, so renting a car as a foreign tourist is entirely possible. (International driving licenses are not accepted in China.)
You can also hire a car with a driver for the day or take the Mutianyu Special Tourism Bus from the Dongzhimen Wai Bus Station.

Getting to Jiankou: Renting a car or booking private transport is recommended. As Xizhazi is a small village, buses are scarce so it can take up to five hours to get there by public transport, as opposed to 90 minutes by car.
Bataizi village sits just inside the Motianling section of the Great Wall and is home to the ruins of a Gothic church built in 1876 under the direction of a German missionary.
The church has been damaged and repaired numerous times in its nearly 150-year history; the bell tower is the only part still standing.
The juxtaposition of its ruins against the rammed-earth Great Wall makes Bataizi a unique place to spend a morning or afternoon.

After finishing your hike along the wall and visiting the church ruins, drop in to the village’s “new” church to say hello to Father Pan; if you speak Chinese, he can answer any questions about the village’s long connection with Catholicism.
Besides Bataizi, Datong should also be on your tourist map; visiting the Yungang Grottoes (a UNESCO world heritage site) and the Hengshan Hanging Temple will make your trip even more memorable.
Late summer is an ideal time to visit Bataizi, as you’ll see a wonderful contrast between the Great Wall and the lush green hills.

Getting there: Bataizi village is 80 kilometers west of Datong, one of Shanxi province’s largest and most famous cities. Zuoyun County is only 22 kilometers away from Bataizi – about a 35-minute drive.
Datong is easily accessible by plane or high-speed train from other cities in China; a taxi from downtown Datong to Bataizi should cost roughly 300 yuan (about $43).
Alternatively, you can make your way to Zuoyun County by bus then hop in a taxi.

In Datong, luxury seekers will want to head for the five-star Yunzhong Traditional Courtyard Hotel. Zuoyun County has one hotel that can accept foreigners: Zuoyun Jinshan International Hotel. Both can be found on popular hotel booking sites.
Laoniuwan (aka the Old Ox Bend Great Wall)
As the locals say, Laoniuwan is where the Great Wall and the mighty Yellow River shake hands.
The Laoniuwan Fortress was built in 1467, while the most famous tower of the Great Wall in this area, Wanghe Tower (literally meaning river-watching tower), was constructed in 1544.
Laoniuwan village is located in Pianguan County, part of Xinzhou city in Shanxi province, just across the river from Inner Mongolia.

Late summer or early fall is a great time to visit, as you’ll avoid the potentially dangerous mountain roads during spring rainstorms, or being uncomfortably cold in a place without great infrastructure.
Along the Great Wall, there are only a few places where it meets bodies of water; of all those, this is the most stunning.
A boat ride along the river is highly recommended. You’ll be able to soak in the natural beauty of the Yellow River Gorge while marveling at the steadfast resolve of these ancient architects.

Getting there: Laoniuwan is difficult to get to by public transportation. The best option is to rent or book a car to take you from Datong to Laoniuwan via Bataizi – this way, you’ll be able to see two incredible locations along the Great Wall in one trip.

Pianguan is the nearest city, about one hour away. Pianguan does not have a train station or an airport. The only option is to arrive by bus. Shuozhou, 140 kilometers from Laoniuwan, has an airport opening later this year.
Construction on the Great Wall in Simatai began in 1373. It was expanded and reinforced periodically throughout the Ming Dynasty.
The Fairy Tower is one of the best-known towers of the wall at Simatai but also one of the least visited due to how difficult it is to access.

Instead, aim to take in incredible views of the Fairy Tower from Wangjing Tower (just a few hundred meters away). It’s a journey that will satiate even the most adventurous hikers, yet can be done without any ropes, ladders or other essential safety gear.

As with a visit to Mutianyu/Jiankou, this section of wall is guaranteed to deliver stunning views any time of year. My only suggestion is to wait for a clear day (usually visibility is great the day after it rains or snows), as the view from Wangjing Tower is unobstructed in every direction.

The hike to the Fairy Tower will leave you in awe of the Northern Barbarians’ supposed determination to reach the capital; the mountains are nearly impassable on foot, let alone by horse, with sheer cliff faces on either side.
It makes for absolutely world-class hiking and an interesting history lesson.

Five-star lodgings are available at Hobo Farm; they also have an incredible restaurant that serves delicious Western and Chinese fare. For 4.5 star lodgings with a lower price tag, try Yatou’s Homestay. Both can be found on major hotel booking sites.
Getting there: Both the Fairy Tower and Wangjing Tower should be accessed via Tangjiazhai village, located in Beijing’s Miyun district.
Tangjiazhai village is 140 kilometers from downtown Beijing, depending on your route. Booking a private car from the city is probably the most time-effective way to get there.
You can also take a high-speed train from Beijing Station to Miyun district and switch to a bus or taxi from there.
Constructed during the reign of Emperor Jiajing (1507-1567), this single-wall section stands seven meters tall in some spots – no small feat considering it was made by piling stones.
It’s located just across the road from the town of Dushikou, in Chicheng in Hebei province.
The piled-stone wall at Dushikou is unique, as many other sections of the Great Wall close to Beijing were constructed using kiln-fired bricks.

Dushikou is best visited in the summer, specifically July and August, when the rolling hills of the surrounding grasslands are peak green. Cool evenings make for perfect outdoor barbecue/bonfire weather.
You’ll be able to find clean and comfortable farmhouse lodgings in Dushikou town; alternatively, Chicheng, 45 minutes away, has a range of hotels to choose from.

Lamb skewers and roast leg of lamb are specialties in these parts, as this part of Hebei is very close to the border with Inner Mongolia. Noodle lovers should also try the local oat noodles, which are delicious.

Getting there: Thanks to all the infrastructure built for the 2022 Winter Olympics, the drive to Dushikou has been shortened by almost two hours. If you prefer not to drive, hop on a bus to Chicheng from the Liuliqiao Transport Hub in Beijing and take a 45-minute taxi ride to Dushikou.
Note that public transportation will take one or two hours longer than private car.

articles.title: Sunny Hostin re-visits 'problematic' Kamala Harris answer on 'The View' as hosts question her 2028 potential

paras.en: "The View" co-host Sunny Hostin revisited her widely-discussed 2024 question to former Vice President Kamala Harris during an event on Monday, calling the former Democratic presidential nominee's answer and refusal to distance herself from former President Joe Biden at the time "problematic."

Brian Teta, the talk show's executive producer and host of its "Behind the Table" podcast, selected the moment as Hostin's most memorable on the show. He said it was a "seminal moment" in the 2024 election cycle.

Hostin described the question as a "gift" and said she thought Harris would have to distance herself from Biden because of his approval ratings at the time. She also said "The View" was the perfect venue to ask the question, calling the liberal show's audience "her people."

"I actually thought the answer was going to be, you know, ‘We had a lot of wins in this administration. I was there for those wins, but I, as a woman of color, as a child of immigrants, as I have a different lived experience, and I intend to bring that lived experience with me into the White House. I will do this. I will do that. I will do this. I will do that. I will do that.’ That was what I was expecting. I was not expecting, 'Not a single thing comes to mind.' And I knew honestly when she said it that it was really problematic," Hostin said.

paras.en: The co-hosts noted that the moment was discussed in books published after the 2024 election, including Harris' memoir, "107 Days," and was also featured in a political ad for President Donald Trump.
In "107 Days," Harris wrote that she had no idea she had just "pulled the pin on a hand grenade," with her answer to Hostin's question. She wrote that her staff was beside themselves.

"Stationed at various places around the set, my staff were beside themselves. Political operatives have an eye to see a moment, and I could kick myself for giving the other side that moment. During the commercial break, while I was having a bit of fun with some young students I’d noticed in the audience who were obviously playing hooky, offering to write notes to their teachers after the show, Opal [Vadhan] passed me a note from our team, telling me to return to that question and mention that a big difference would be that I would put a Republican in my cabinet," she wrote in her book.

paras.en: Teta and the co-hosts said they all knew her response was going to be a problem.
Co-host Ana Navarro said Harris' staff "ran" because staff members knew immediately that Harris needed to return to the question and address her answer.
During the show on Friday, both Navarro and Haines said they wouldn't tell Harris not to run, but questioned if she would be the best option for the Democratic Party.

"If the Democrats want to win, I don't think she's the right candidate because I think the Democrats have been screaming for new energy. They've been saying we need something new to combat this. This would be her third time on this ballot. From the first time when she didn't ... she was out really early when she ran, and then the time with Biden, this would be the third time. People are clamoring for fresh energy, and there's a lot of candidates," Haines said.

Co-host Joy Behar has said on several occasions that she doesn't think the U.S. would elect a woman as president, citing Harris and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton's losses to Trump. She has said the 2028 Democratic presidential nominee should be a man if the party wants to win.
Hostin questioned whether president would be the right position for Harris during an April episode of "The View" and said she wished Harris had pursued a run for California governor.

"This goes right to the heart of what the Media Research Center has been arguing to the FCC about for months now. The View knowingly operates as a propaganda arm for the Democratic Party and for Democratic candidates," NewsBusters associate editor Nicholas Fondacaro told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Sunny openly admitted that her intention with the question was to help Kamala with what she felt was a layup question that would lead to a slam-dunk answer. This incident was an abuse of ABC's privileged access to the public broadcast spectrum."
